lesson.title: Your Single Best Guess
lesson.summary: A point estimate is a single number, computed from a sample, used as the best available guess for an unknown population parameter.
lesson.body:
The simplest form of statistical inference is also the most intuitive: take a sample statistic and use it directly as your best guess for the corresponding population parameter. That single number is called a point estimate. A sample proportion p-hat is the point estimate of the population proportion p. A sample mean x-bar is the point estimate of the population mean mu. A sample standard deviation s is commonly used as the point estimate of the population standard deviation sigma.

Point estimates are useful precisely because they are simple and direct, and under reasonable conditions, like random sampling, they tend to be unbiased, meaning that if you imagine repeating the sampling process over and over, the statistic's average value across all those samples equals the true parameter. That property, which comes straight from the properties of the sampling distribution, is part of why we trust point estimates as a starting point at all: they do not systematically overshoot or undershoot the truth.

But a point estimate, on its own, is incomplete. It gives no indication of how far off it might be. A p-hat of 0.25 computed from a sample of 10 people carries far less information than a p-hat of 0.25 computed from a sample of 10,000, yet the point estimate alone looks identical in both cases. This is the central limitation that motivates the next chapter: a point estimate needs to be paired with some measure of its precision to be genuinely useful for inference.

Return to the transit survey: 400 randomly sampled adults, 100 of whom support the measure. The point estimate of the population proportion p is p-hat equals 100 divided by 400 equals 0.25, or 25%. That is the single best guess a statistician would report for the true proportion of all adults in the city who support the measure. It is almost certainly not exactly correct, the true value of p might be 23%, or 27%, or something else entirely, but among all possible single numbers, 0.25 is the one best supported by the sample data. The natural next question, how far off this guess might be, is answered by moving from a point estimate to an interval estimate, which is exactly where the next chapter picks up.
